CHAPTER 4.1 · LEARNING AREA 4 · APRIL · MAY

Multi-stage random experiments

Drawing twice, rolling three times, a survey with two questions: many random experiments run in stages. With the tree diagram and the path rules you keep track, with the two-way table you sort two characteristics, and with stochastic independence you clarify whether two events have anything to do with each other. And where calculating is hard, simulation helps.

6 LESSONS2 UNITSSIMULATIONHISTORY
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • describe multi-stage random experiments with the urn model, with and without replacement
  • calculate probabilities with the tree diagram and the path rules and estimate them with the complementary event
  • simulate random experiments
  • set up and read two-way tables
  • check events for stochastic independence and discuss different ways of solving a problem

UNIT 13 LESSONS

1Urn model, tree diagram and path rules

With replacement, the probability of red is $\tfrac{3}{5}$ for every draw, so for red twice it is $\tfrac{3}{5} \cdot \tfrac{3}{5} = \tfrac{9}{25} = 0.36$. Without replacement, after the first red ball there are only 2 red balls among 4: $\tfrac{3}{5} \cdot \tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{3}{10} = 0.3$. In the tree diagram each branch carries the probability of that stage, and a route through the tree is called a path.

KEY POINT · PATH RULES

1st path rule (product rule): The probability of a path is the product of the probabilities along the path.

2nd path rule (sum rule): The probability of an event is the sum of the probabilities of its paths.

Urn model: With replacement the probabilities stay the same; without replacement they change from stage to stage.

Complementary event: $P(\text{at least once}) = 1 - P(\text{never})$, often the shortest way.

Check: The sum of all path probabilities is 1, and so is the sum of the branches at each fork.

Simulation: With random digits 0 to 9 you simulate $p = 0.3$ by counting 0, 1, 2 as success. Many runs estimate the probability.

INTERACTIVE · TREE DIAGRAM WORKSHOP

Set up the urn, choose with or without replacement and click on the ends of paths to put together an event.

EXAMPLE 1 · EXACTLY ONE RED

Two draws without replacement from 3 red and 2 blue balls. How likely is exactly one red ball?

Two paths: red–blue $\tfrac{3}{5} \cdot \tfrac{2}{4}$ and blue–red $\tfrac{2}{5} \cdot \tfrac{3}{4}$.

$\tfrac{6}{20} + \tfrac{6}{20} =$ $\tfrac{3}{5}$.

EXAMPLE 2 · AT LEAST ONE SIX

A dice is rolled four times. How likely is at least one six?

Complementary event “no six”: $\left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^4 \approx 0.482$.

$1 - 0.482 \approx 0.518$: a little more than half.

EXERCISES

Urn with 3 red and 2 blue balls. Calculate for drawing twice: a) with replacement, two different colours   b) with replacement, at least one blue   c) drawing three times without replacement, red three times

a) $\tfrac{12}{25}$   b) $\tfrac{16}{25}$   c) $\tfrac{3}{5} \cdot \tfrac{2}{4} \cdot \tfrac{1}{3} = \tfrac{1}{10}$

Two dice: how likely is a total of 7, how likely a double?

Both $\tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac{1}{6}$.

60% of the students at a large school come by bus. Two are chosen at random. How likely is it that exactly one of them comes by bus? Why may you calculate here as if with replacement?

$2 \cdot 0.6 \cdot 0.4 = 0.48$. With many people, one selection hardly changes the proportion.

What is the smallest number of rolls needed so that at least one six comes up with a probability of at least 90%? Try it with the CAS.

$1 - \left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^n \geq 0.9$: $n = 13$ (for $n = 12$ only about 0.888).

Plan a simulation with random digits for: “A spinner shows red with 30%; how likely is red at least twice in 5 spins?” Carry out 20 runs and compare with the calculation $1 - 0.7^5 - 5 \cdot 0.3 \cdot 0.7^4 \approx 0.47$.

Five digits each time, success for 0, 1, 2; count how often at least two successes occur. With 20 runs the result spreads noticeably around 0.47.

UNIT 23 LESSONS

2Two-way table and stochastic independence

Of 100 people asked, 60 do sport ($S$), 40 make music ($M$), 30 do both. The two-way table contains the four combinations, with the totals in the margins. If sport and music were independent of each other, 40% of the 60 sporty people, i.e. 24, would have to make music. But there are 30. So the two characteristics are related in this group: $P(S \cap M) = 0.3 \neq 0.6 \cdot 0.4 = 0.24$.

KEY POINT · TWO-WAY TABLE AND INDEPENDENCE

The two-way table contains $P(A \cap B)$, $P(A \cap \overline{B})$, $P(\overline{A} \cap B)$, $P(\overline{A} \cap \overline{B})$; the row and column totals give $P(A)$, $P(\overline{A})$, $P(B)$, $P(\overline{B})$, and the grand total is 1.

$A$ and $B$ are called stochastically independent if $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$, otherwise dependent. Then $\overline{A}$ and $B$ etc. are independent as well.

Intuitively: the proportion of $B$ is the same in group $A$ as in group $\overline{A}$.

Mutually exclusive ($A \cap B = \emptyset$) is something different: with positive probabilities, mutually exclusive events are actually dependent.

Tree ↔ table: In the tree, $P(A \cap B)$ is the product along the path $A$, then $B$; in the table it is directly in its cell.

Dependent does not mean causal: A relationship in the data does not say what the cause is. Perhaps sporty people simply have more time in the afternoon.

INTERACTIVE · INDEPENDENT OR NOT?

Set $P(A)$, $P(B)$ and $P(A \cap B)$. The two-way table and the unit square show when the events are independent.

EXAMPLE 3 · COMPLETING THE TABLE

$P(A) = 0.4$, $P(B) = 0.5$, $P(A \cap B) = 0.2$. Complete the table and check for independence.

$P(A \cap \overline{B}) = 0.2$, $P(\overline{A} \cap B) = 0.3$, $P(\overline{A} \cap \overline{B}) = 0.3$.

$0.4 \cdot 0.5 = 0.2 = P(A \cap B)$: independent.

EXAMPLE 4 · CALCULATING WITH INDEPENDENCE

$A$ and $B$ are independent with $P(A) = 0.3$ and $P(B) = 0.5$. Find $P(A \cap B)$, $P(A \cup B)$ and $P(\overline{A} \cap \overline{B})$.

$P(A \cap B) = 0.15$, $P(A \cup B) = 0.3 + 0.5 - 0.15 = 0.65$.

$P(\overline{A} \cap \overline{B}) = 0.7 \cdot 0.5 = 0.35$ $= 1 - 0.65$.

TRAINING · COMPLETING TWO-WAY TABLES

Fill in the missing cells. You can ask for a new table.

EXERCISES

Of 200 people, 80 wear glasses, 120 are women, and 50 women wear glasses. Set up the two-way table with absolute numbers.

woman/glasses 50, woman/none 70, man/glasses 30, man/none 50; totals 120, 80, 80, 120, 200.

Are “woman” and “glasses” independent in this group? Compare the proportions wearing glasses among women and men.

Women $\tfrac{50}{120} \approx 41.7\%$, men $\tfrac{30}{80} = 37.5\%$; $0.6 \cdot 0.4 = 0.24 \neq 0.25$: slightly dependent.

Two dice: $A$ “first dice shows 6”, $B$ “total 7”. Are $A$ and $B$ independent?

$P(A) = \tfrac{1}{6}$, $P(B) = \tfrac{1}{6}$, $P(A \cap B) = P(\{(6,1)\}) = \tfrac{1}{36}$: independent, although you would not expect it.

$A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive with $P(A) = 0.3$ and $P(B) = 0.4$. Find $P(A \cup B)$ and show that they are dependent.

$P(A \cup B) = 0.7$; $P(A \cap B) = 0 \neq 0.12$.

Solve Example 4 in two ways: with the addition rule and with the complementary event. Discuss which way is quicker.

Addition rule: $0.3 + 0.5 - 0.15 = 0.65$. Complementary event: $1 - 0.7 \cdot 0.5 = 0.65$. For independent events the second way is often shorter.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A spinner shows red with probability $\tfrac{1}{4}$, otherwise green. It is spun twice. Give all paths with their probabilities.

RR $\tfrac{1}{16}$, RG $\tfrac{3}{16}$, GR $\tfrac{3}{16}$, GG $\tfrac{9}{16}$.

Connecting with Year 10: The random variable $X$ counts the red balls when drawing twice with replacement from 3 red and 2 blue. Give the distribution and $E(X)$.

$P(X = 0) = 0.16$, $P(X = 1) = 0.48$, $P(X = 2) = 0.36$; $E(X) = 0.48 + 0.72 = 1.2$.

A dice is rolled ten times. First estimate, then calculate: how likely is at least one six?

$1 - \left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^{10} \approx 0.84$.

Education for sustainable development: in a town, 30% cycle to work. Among the under-30s it is 45%, and they make up 20% of the working population. Draw up a two-way table and check whether age and cycling are independent.

Young and bike: $0.2 \cdot 0.45 = 0.09$; young without bike 0.11; older with bike $0.3 - 0.09 = 0.21$; older without bike 0.59. $0.2 \cdot 0.3 = 0.06 \neq 0.09$: dependent.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

The Chevalier de Méré's wager

The French writer and gambler Antoine Gombaud, known as the Chevalier de Méré, knew a good bet: in four rolls of one dice, at least one six comes up. He thought a second bet was just as good: in 24 rolls of two dice, at least one double six comes up. His reasoning: $\tfrac{4}{6} = \tfrac{24}{36}$. But in the long run he lost with it.

In 1654 he put his questions to Blaise Pascal, who exchanged letters about them with Pierre de Fermat. This correspondence is regarded as the beginning of probability theory. With the complementary event it is easy: $1 - \left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^4 \approx 51.8\%$, but $1 - \left(\tfrac{35}{36}\right)^{24} \approx 49.1\%$. The first bet is favourable, the second narrowly unfavourable.

Source: D. R. Bellhouse, C. Genest, “Antoine Gombaud, Chevalier de Méré”, Statistical Science 39 (2024), no. 3. The correspondence between Pascal and Fermat dates from 1654.
